rationale: This is a clear, clinically grounded PTSD vignette with a strong personal narrative and highly identifiable symptoms linked to a traumatic medical crisis involving her child. It explicitly includes intrusion-like emotional re-experiencing, avoidance, hypervigilance, startle, guilt, anger, trigger reactivity, and functional impairment, while also capturing cognitive-model features such as ongoing threat, negative appraisals, fragmented memory, and maladaptive coping. A minor limitation is that the traumatic event is a medical trauma rather than a prototypical violence/disaster scenario, but it is still presented in a plausible and clinically representative way.

This is a clear, clinically credible PTSD vignette centered on combat-related trauma, with strong narrative detail rather than a checklist style. It explicitly includes Criterion A exposure, intrusive fragmented sensory memories and nightmares, avoidance, negative mood/cognitions, hyperarousal, triggers, and functional strain at work and in relationships. A particular strength is the sense of ongoing current threat and the description of fragmented trauma memory; the only minor limitation is that impairment is somewhat subtle because she remains outwardly high functioning.

This is a very clear, clinically rich, and highly representative PTSD vignette with explicit traumatic exposure, sensory intrusions, avoidance, negative appraisals, hyperarousal, and clear occupational impairment. It is especially strong in depicting Ehlers & Clark-maintaining processes—current sense of threat, trigger-linked re-experiencing, fragmented/alien trauma memory, and maladaptive coping—while remaining coherent and narrative rather than checklist-like.

This vignette is highly clear, clinically grounded, and strongly representative of chronic PTSD, with explicit coverage of Criterion A trauma exposure, intrusion, avoidance, negative cognitions/mood, hyperarousal, and functional impairment. It also vividly illustrates maintaining processes from Ehlers and Clark’s model, including a persistent sense of current threat, negative appraisals, sensory-laden re-experiencing triggered by cues, and avoidance/safety behaviors; the only minor limitation is that it is somewhat polished and comprehensive compared with how patients may present spontaneously.

This is a highly clear, clinically plausible PTSD vignette with a strong personal narrative and good grounding in contemporary cognitive models, especially persistent threat, safety behaviors, and avoidance. It clearly describes Criterion A trauma exposure, hypervigilance, avoidance, negative emotional constriction, and functional/interpersonal impact; a relative weakness is that classic intrusion symptoms and altered trauma-memory features are not explicitly described.

This vignette is clearly written, clinically relevant, and presented as a coherent personal narrative with explicit trauma exposure, triggers, avoidance, negative beliefs/distrust, and functional impairment. It is somewhat representative of PTSD, but hyperarousal symptoms are not clearly described, and some elements (such as generalized distrust and the polished explanatory style) feel somewhat less grounded or overly constructed compared with typical clinical presentations.
